compound eyes are arranged along the radioles or at the
extreme tips (Bok et al., 2016; Bok et al., 2017). Each compound
eye is comprised of up to 50 separate units called ommatidia.
Each ommatidium is composed of three cells: one receptor
cell forming a ciliary receptive segment, and two pigment
cells surrounding an extracellular lens (crystalline cone). The
eyes cannot form images but are extremely sensitive to visual
motion because, in concert, they cover such a wide area. Any
motion will trigger retraction into the tube (Nilsson, 1994).

Lateral organs are internally ciliated pits or ciliated papillae
present segmentally between the notopodia and neuropodia,
or dorsal to the neuropodia when notopodia are missing (Figs.
2.7c, d). Lateral organs are known in the following major
taxa: Apistobranchidae, Capitellidae, Magelona, Maldanomorpha,
Opheliidae, Orbiniidae, Paraonidae, Scalibregmatidae, Spionidae,
and Terebelliformia (Purschke and Hausen, 2007; Rullier, 1951).
‘They may be present in Amphinomida (Purschke, 2005). Giv-
en this phylogenetic distribution they may represent conver-
gently acquired structures or have been lost repeatedly within
Annelida (Beckers et al., 2019a). Hayashi and Yamane (1994,

1997) described a probable sensory structure which they called
the dorsal cirrus organ. It is a ciliated structure on the lower
side of the notopodia in most Eunicida. These structures may
well be homologous with lateral organs and should be further
investigated (Purschke and Hausen, 2007; Rouse and Plejjel,
2001).

In most annelids there are usually two fluid systems, the coclom,
and the circulatory system, and both (if present) are involved in
the excretion of waste products. To achieve this excretion, there
must be ducts to the exterior and these are generally referred
to as nephridia, Two different kinds of filtration nephridia
are described in Annelida: protonephridia and metanephridia.
During the development of an annelid, larval protonephridia
generally precede segmentally arranged metanephridia. The
first pair of larval protonephridia that develop are also called
head-kidneys (Hatschek, 1878). In annelids, the inner end of
a nephridium projects or opens into the coelom of the seg-
ment in front of the one in which the nephridiopore is located.
